title: Acute otitis media (child)
subject: paediatrics
setting: Primary care, emergency department, paediatric outpatients
summary: Diagnose AOM only with a bulging tympanic membrane or new otorrhoea (or mild bulging with recent otalgia or intense erythema). Always treat pain. Give high-dose amoxicillin 80 to 90 mg/kg/day for otorrhoea, severe symptoms or bilateral AOM under 2 years; otherwise offer observation with review at 48 to 72 hours.

sections.title: Diagnosis (AAP, age 6 months to 12 years)
items: Diagnose AOM with moderate to severe bulging of the tympanic membrane, or new otorrhoea not caused by otitis externa.
Also diagnose with mild bulging plus ear pain of recent onset (under 48 hours; holding, tugging or rubbing the ear in a non-verbal child) or intense erythema of the tympanic membrane.

Do not diagnose AOM without a middle ear effusion (check with pneumatic otoscopy or tympanometry). A red drum alone from crying or fever is not AOM, and otitis media with effusion does not need antibiotics.
Severe AOM: moderate or severe otalgia, otalgia for 48 hours or more, or temperature 39 °C or higher.

Complications needing urgent assessment: swelling, redness or tenderness behind the ear or a protruding pinna (mastoiditis), facial nerve palsy, severe headache, neck stiffness, vertigo, reduced consciousness or a toxic child.

sections.title: Pain relief and the antibiotic decision
items: Assess and treat pain in every child with paracetamol or ibuprofen, whether or not an antibiotic is given.
Give antibiotics at any age from 6 months with otorrhoea or severe symptoms, and for bilateral AOM at 6 to 23 months.
Unilateral non-severe AOM at 6 to 23 months, and any non-severe AOM at 2 years and over: antibiotic or observation, decided jointly with the parents.
Observation needs a follow-up plan: start antibiotics (or use a back-up prescription) if the child worsens or fails to improve within 48 to 72 hours.
Infants under 6 months are outside the AAP guideline: keep a low threshold for antibiotics and paediatric review. A febrile infant under 3 months follows the fever in under 5s pathway.

sections.title: Antibiotic choice and duration
items: First line: high-dose amoxicillin 80 to 90 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (max 2 g per dose), unless amoxicillin was taken in the past 30 days, there is purulent conjunctivitis, or the child is penicillin allergic.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin with 6.4 mg/kg/day clavulanate in 2 doses) if amoxicillin was taken in the past 30 days, with purulent conjunctivitis (suggests Haemophilus influenzae), or for recurrent AOM unresponsive to amoxicillin.

Penicillin allergy: cefdinir, cefuroxime axetil or ceftriaxone (see drugs). Macrolides are not recommended unless there is severe allergy to both penicillins and cephalosporins, because resistance and treatment failure are common.
Duration: 10 days under 2 years or with severe symptoms; 7 days at 2 to 5 years and 5 to 7 days at 6 years and over for non-severe AOM.

sections.title: Review at 48 to 72 hours
items: If worse or not better after 48 to 72 hours, re-examine to confirm AOM and exclude other causes.
Step up: observation to amoxicillin; amoxicillin to amoxicillin-clavulanate; amoxicillin-clavulanate to ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM or IV daily for 3 days, and consider ENT referral for tympanocentesis.
A middle ear effusion often persists for weeks after AOM; it does not need further antibiotics.

sections.title: Recurrent AOM and other groups
items: Recurrent AOM: 3 episodes in 6 months, or 4 in 12 months with at least 1 in the past 6 months. Do not give prophylactic antibiotics; tympanostomy tubes may be offered (refer to ENT).
Children with tympanostomy tubes, craniofacial anomalies, immunodeficiency or cochlear implants are outside this guideline: seek ENT advice.
Ear discharge through a perforation lasting more than 2 weeks suggests chronic suppurative otitis media, which is common in India: refer to ENT rather than repeating oral antibiotics.

sections.title: Prevention
items: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine as per the national schedule.
Annual influenza vaccine for children from 6 months of age.
Exclusive breastfeeding for at least 6 months, and no exposure to tobacco smoke.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Diagnosing AOM from a red drum in a crying or febrile child without bulging or effusion.
Low-dose amoxicillin, which may fail against less penicillin-sensitive pneumococci.
Routine macrolide use despite high resistance.
Missing mastoiditis or intracranial spread in a child who stays unwell despite antibiotics.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin
drugs.dose: 80 to 90 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses (max 2 g per dose); 10 days under 2 years or severe, 7 days at 2 to 5 years, 5 to 7 days at 6 years and over

drugs.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate
drugs.dose: 90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin with 6.4 mg/kg/day clavulanate orally in 2 divided doses (max 2 g amoxicillin per dose) for 10 days
drugs.notes: Amoxicillin in the past 30 days, purulent conjunctivitis, or failure of amoxicillin. The 14:1 ratio limits clavulanate-related diarrhoea; with lower-ratio products, give part of the dose as plain amoxicillin.

drugs.name: Cefdinir
drugs.dose: 14 mg/kg/day orally in 1 or 2 doses (max 600 mg/day)
drugs.notes: Penicillin allergy; duration as for amoxicillin.

drugs.name: Cefuroxime axetil
drugs.dose: 30 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses (max 500 mg per dose)
drugs.notes: Penicillin allergy; duration as for amoxicillin.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: 50 mg/kg IM or IV once daily (max 2 g per dose) for 1 to 3 days; 3 days after treatment failure
drugs.notes: Penicillin allergy, vomiting, or failure of oral treatment.

drugs.name: Ibuprofen
drugs.dose: 10 mg/kg orally every 6 to 8 hours (max 30 mg/kg/day; max 400 mg per dose)

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg orally every 4 to 6 hours (max 4 doses and 60 mg/kg in 24 hours; max 1 g per dose)
